our_perspective: An awards jury reads a house the way we try to design one: in plan first, then in section, then in light. A photograph can flatter a facade; it cannot invent a coherent sequence of rooms. That is why we begin from typology rather than image: the courtyard, the portico, the pergola, elements Italian domestic architecture refined from Villa Adriana to Palladio's La Rotonda. In Los Angeles those forms also do climate work. Transsolar calibrates cross-ventilation for the city's west-to-east winds, and exposed walls carry thermal mass. Our four typologies are starting points, not catalog designs. We hold them to the test a peer jury applies: does the plan earn the picture?
body_html:
Residential Design magazine has announced the winners of its 2026 Residential Design Architecture Awards. The program is one of the few national recognitions devoted entirely to houses. It is also one of the few where the judges are working residential architects rather than tastemakers or sales professionals. This year's panel had five members, each a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects, described by the magazine as "talented architects with deep expertise in residential architecture."

Source: Residential Design, "The Winners of the 2026 Residential Design Architecture Awards"

Who Judged, and Why It Matters

The announcement names the jury in full. Among the jurors are Katherine Chia, FAIA, of Desai Chia Architecture in New York, and Anne Mooney, FAIA, of Sparano + Mooney Architecture, which practices from Los Angeles and Salt Lake City (Residential Design). The complete list of winning projects and the jury's commentary is published at the source. We refer readers there rather than paraphrase project credits secondhand.

5FAIA architects on the 2026 judging panel
2Named jurors practicing in New York and Los Angeles/Salt Lake City

The composition is the first data point worth reading. Fellowship in the AIA is the profession's recognition of sustained contribution, conferred by peers. A jury made up entirely of Fellows judges a house on terms a client rarely sees in a listing: how the plan organizes daily life, how the section handles light and height, how the structure and the finished surface relate, and whether a detail was resolved or merely concealed.

The geography is the second. A Los Angeles-connected practice on the panel means at least one juror works daily with the conditions that shape Southern California houses. That includes hillside sections, strong sun, the long indoor-outdoor tradition from the Case Study era onward, and an increasingly demanding regulatory context.

A listing photograph sells an image. A peer jury examines a plan.

What This Means for Los Angeles Clients

For anyone commissioning a serious house in Malibu, Beverly Hills or the Westside, juried residential awards are a more useful benchmark than market headlines. Price per square foot reports what a house traded for. It says nothing about whether the rooms are well proportioned, whether the courtyard actually ventilates, or whether the envelope will look as good in twenty years as on the day it was photographed.

Read with a practicing architect's eye, awards like these reward legibility more than spectacle. That means a clear parti, a limited and honest material palette, and openings placed for light and view rather than for facade composition. Those are the same qualities that tend to age well. They also hold up against the technical demands now placed on new construction in California, because a coherent plan absorbs constraints that a styled one has to disguise.

The practical advice for a client is simple. Before choosing an architect, study the plans and sections behind a portfolio, not only the photographs. Then ask the question a jury would ask: what idea organizes this house, and does every room serve it?

Looking Ahead

Residential architecture in California is entering a period in which design ambition and technical rigor can no longer be separated. Programs judged by architects for architects keep the conversation anchored in the discipline itself, in typology, proportion, light and craft. That anchor will matter more as Los Angeles rebuilds and reinvents its most prized neighborhoods. Clients who learn to read a house the way these jurors do will commission better ones.
